name: Hewes Crab

origin.parentage: Unknown; it is sometimes suggested to carry native American crab (Malus angustifolia) ancestry, but this is unproven

history: Virginia's classic colonial cider apple, described in the early nineteenth century from trees that were already said to be about a century old. It was planted at Monticello and on many Virginia plantations, and is now prized again by American craft cider makers.

look.description: Very small crab-like fruit, about 4 cm across, dull green streaked and overlaid with purplish dull red and peppered with pale dots.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, very juicy flesh that is sharply acidic with a noticeable astringent, slightly bitter edge. Too austere for most people raw; its value is a clear, dry, well-structured cider, on its own or in blends.
taste.best_eaten: Pressed Oct-Nov, after a short sweat

tree.notes: Long-lived, hardy tree that crops heavily but with a strong tendency to alternate years; thinning in the 'on' year helps even it out.

pollination.notes: Listed as group 3 and a good pollinator, with some self-fertility claimed; crops are better with a partner nearby.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer eastern US climates such as Virginia and the Mid-Atlantic, and also cold northern orchards where its hardiness counts.
climate.poor_climates: Few clear weaknesses recorded; in cool, cloudy summers the juice will be sharper and thinner.

health.other: Generally regarded as a tough, long-lived tree; main drawback is biennial bearing. Specific disease ratings are not well documented.

grow_notes: A good backbone tree for a cider orchard in a cold or hot-summer area. Thin heavy crops to reduce alternate bearing, and blend its sharp, tannic juice with sweeter apples.

name: Smokehouse

origin.place: Mill Creek, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, USA
origin.parentage: Said to be a seedling of Vandevere; not confirmed

history: Arose in the 1830s on William Gibbons' farm near Mill Creek in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, from a tree growing beside his smokehouse, which gave it its name. It spread through Pennsylvania and the Mid-Atlantic as an all-purpose farm apple.

look.description: Fairly large, flattish fruit, greenish-yellow shaded and striped with red.

taste.summary: Crisp, moderately fine-grained yellowish flesh with a sweet, honeyed, fresh-cider flavour balanced by some sharpness; some tasters find it almost candy-sweet, and individual fruit can be soft or dry. Keeps well through March and is very good for pies, crisps and drying.

tree.notes: Spur-bearing; other tree characteristics are not well documented.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded; provide a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mid-Atlantic and lower Northeast climates with cold winters and warm summers, like south-east Pennsylvania.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; climate values are inferred from its region of origin.

grow_notes: A dependable dual-purpose farmstead apple for cold-winter, warm-summer regions. Plant with a pollinator and use the fruit for eating and baking through early winter.

name: Sheepnose
history: Sheepnose is the common rural name, especially in Vermont and Pennsylvania, for the apple pomologists call Black Gilliflower, an eighteenth-century New England variety probably from Connecticut. The southern Crow's Egg is widely thought to be the same apple. Named for its long, tapering, nose-like shape.

look.description: Distinctive tall, tapering, ribbed fruit with dark red skin deepening to almost black-purple, with faint darker stripes.

taste.summary: Greenish-white, firm flesh that is sweet and mild, with a distinctive perfume and a dry, nutty character. Opinion is split: some find it crisp and fragrant, others dry and cardboard-like with little juice. It hangs late on the tree but turns dry and fibrous if over-ripe or stored, so use it fairly soon; traditionally baked or dried.

tree.notes: Spur-bearing and reported to crop prolifically; fruit hangs well but must not be left to over-ripen.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter New England and northern Mid-Atlantic climates, where it is regarded as a hardy variety.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid climates are likely to give poorer colour and quicker drying out of the flesh; inferred from origin.

health.other: Main fault is flesh that becomes dry and mealy if picked late or stored too long.

grow_notes: Hardy and productive in cold-winter areas. Pick promptly when coloured and use for baking, drying and early-winter eating rather than long storage.

name: Magnum Bonum

origin.parentage: Seedling grown from seed of the Hall apple

history: Raised in 1828 in Davidson County, North Carolina, when John Kinney planted seeds of the Hall apple. It became a long-standing southern favourite for early autumn and was grown commercially in Virginia for a time.

look.description: Small to medium yellow apple largely covered with light and dark red streaks and many small pale dots.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, crisp, juicy white flesh, often pink-stained under the skin, with a well-flavoured, aromatic sweet-sharp balance; one grower in England found it a little sharper than Cox. Regarded as one of the best early-autumn southern dessert apples.

tree.notes: Described as a hardy and productive tree; other details are not well documented.

climate.best_climates: The piedmont and mountains of the upper South (North Carolina, Virginia), with hot summers and moderate winters; reported to do well in mild south-west England too.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; chill and hardiness figures are inferred from its North Carolina origin.

grow_notes: A good early-autumn dessert apple for warm-summer regions. Plant with a pollinator of similar season; the fruit keeps reasonably for a few weeks if stored cool.

name: Yates
history: Found around 1844 by Matthew Yates in Fayette County, Georgia, and widely grown across the South for its exceptional keeping. Valued as a winter eating apple and as a cider apple, and reported to grow well from the southern mountains down to the coastal plain.

look.description: Small to very small fruit, pale yellow almost hidden under dark red shading and stripes; flesh sometimes tinged red under the skin.

taste.summary: Pleasant, sweetish yellowish-white flesh, usually described as tender, juicy and aromatic, though one modern grower found it crisp and fairly dry with a tangy flavour suggesting blood orange. Holds its quality through the winter and is well regarded for cider as well as fresh eating.

pollination.notes: Listed as a group 4 diploid in one database; plant with a compatible pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Hot-summer, mild-winter regions of the American South, from the Georgia piedmont to the coastal plain.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short-season climates such as Britain may not ripen this very late apple; chill and hardiness are estimates inferred from its Georgia origin.

health.other: Disease profile not documented in sources checked; its long popularity in the humid South suggests reasonable tolerance, but this is unverified.

grow_notes: One of the best choices for a long-keeping apple in a warm southern garden. Leave the fruit on the tree as late as possible and store it cool for eating through late winter.
